transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Yeah, thanks for seeing me. I just... I don't even really know where to start, but I came in because I just can’t stop thinking about my face. Specifically, the left side of my face. It just looks completely off. Like, my nose and my jaw, they're... they're crooked. And it's not just a little bit, it's so glaringly obvious to me. 

I first really started fixating on it when I was looking at my ID photos, and then it got so much worse with my online classes. Whenever the camera is on, I can't even pay attention to the lecture because I'm just staring at my own square on the screen, looking at how warped my jawline is on that left side. The lens just captures exactly how asymmetrical it is. And the thing is, I've brought it up to a few people, and they always say they don’t see it, or they tell me it's all in my head, which honestly just makes me feel worse because it is *right there*. 

It's gotten to the point where it's affecting my job. I'm a CNC programmer, so I'm in the machining lab a lot, and the fluorescent lighting in there is so harsh. I just feel like every single person in the CNC lab is staring at it. I'll be setting up a really complex tool path, doing genuinely good work, but I just know—I can feel it—that everyone is noticing my crooked face before they ever notice my work. It's just exhausting. I can't turn the thoughts off, no matter what I'm doing, I'm just always thinking about how everyone is looking at my jaw.
Are you avoiding any social interactions or activities outside of work because of concerns about your appearance?

Yeah... yeah, I am. I mean, it's not just outside of work, it's kind of everything right now. Like, outside of work, I used to play soccer. Just, you know, intramural stuff, pickup games with some guys from my classes, but I completely stopped going. I just couldn't handle the idea of being out on the field, running around, and having people looking at me from all different angles. You know, when you're moving around like that, you can't control how the sun hits your face, and I just kept thinking about how terrible and lopsided my jaw must look to everyone on the sidelines or the other team. And I used to volunteer, too, at this community center doing some basic tech stuff for them, but I had to quit that as well. I just... I don't want people looking at me. I really don't. I can't stand the thought of them analyzing my face while I'm trying to talk to them or help them with an issue. 

But it's actually even worse than just the social stuff, honestly, because it's bleeding into my actual program. Like, I’ve been missing my CNC labs and my shop shifts. There are mornings where I wake up, and I make the mistake of looking in the bathroom mirror, and I just... I get stuck. I'll spend an hour just staring at how crooked the left side of my face is, trying to see if maybe I can hold my head a certain way or tilt my chin to hide it, but nothing works. And then I just feel so awful that I literally can’t get myself out the door. I'll just sit on the edge of my bed and let the clock run out on my shift because the anxiety of being seen is just too heavy. 

It's gotten so bad that my faculty mentor actually pulled me aside recently. He told me that my work placement could be in jeopardy if I keep missing these shop hours. And I know how important this placement is for my career—like, it's everything if you want to get a good programming job out of school—but even knowing that, even knowing I could lose my spot and mess up my whole future, I still can't bring myself to go in when I feel like everyone is just staring at my jaw. I just can't do it.
Are there any other areas of your life, aside from work and social interactions, where your concerns about your face are affecting your ability to function or causing you distress?

Well, I mean, it's... it's just exhausting, you know? It's not just the missing out on things or the fear of being seen. It's the actual process of trying to get ready to be seen, if that makes sense. Like, the mornings are just a complete nightmare. I mentioned getting stuck looking in the mirror, but it's not just a quick glance. I'll get in the bathroom before I leave for school, and I'll start checking the left side of my face. And then I have to pull out my phone camera, because the mirror flips the image, right? So I need to see what everyone else is seeing. I'll take a picture, then I'll switch to the video setting and sort of pan around my face, trying to catch the exact angle where the lopsidedness is the most obvious. 

And then I start trying to fix it. I'll spend God knows how long messing with my hair, trying to see if parting it differently or pulling it forward will somehow balance out my jaw. Sometimes I'll change my shirt three or four times, thinking maybe a different collar will distract from my neck and my chin. And I know it sounds crazy, but I can't stop. I just keep checking and checking. 

I even drag my mom into it. I'll go downstairs and I'll ask her, "Does my jaw look weird today? Is it really noticeable?" And she always sighs and says no, but I don't believe her, so I'll ask her again a few minutes later. I'll ask her to look at me from the left side, then the right side. It's like I need her to confirm what I'm seeing, but when she doesn't, it just makes me panic more. 

And by the time I've done all of this—the mirror checking, the phone camera, the hair, the shirts, interrogating my mom—so much time has passed. Like I said before, sometimes I just miss my lab entirely because I've spent an hour and a half just standing in the bathroom. Or, if I do manage to force myself out the door, I'm just completely drained. I'll show up to the CNC lab, and I'm supposed to be writing G-code or setting up a machine, and my brain is just totally wiped out from the sheer stress of the morning routine. I can't focus on the numbers or the tool paths because I've already spent all my energy just trying to make my face look presentable enough to walk out the front door. It's just... it takes over everything.
Do you feel like you have to perform any specific routines or rituals to try to feel better about your face before you can leave the house or be around others?

Yeah, exactly. I mean, like I was just saying a minute ago, it really is a whole... process. I guess you could definitely call it a routine, or a ritual, because if I don't do it, I literally can't leave the house. It's like I'm trapped in this loop every single morning before I leave for school. 

I get completely stuck in the bathroom. It always starts with the mirror, just leaning in really close, checking the jawline, trying to see how bad it is that day. But the mirror isn't enough, because it flips the image, so then I have to pull out my phone camera. I do the photos, then the video panning, because I have to know exactly how bad the angle is from everyone else's perspective. I just stand there analyzing the footage, zooming in on the left side of my face.

Then I move on to trying to fix it, or at least hide it. I'll spend forever messing with my hair, trying to get it to fall just right over the side of my face to shadow the crookedness, or I'm tearing through my closet changing shirts over and over again, trying to find a collar that might somehow camouflage the lopsidedness. I'll put on a crew neck, take it off, try a polo, take it off, try a hoodie... just hoping something will make a difference.

And then the final step of the routine is always my mom. I have to go ask her if it looks weird. I'll go downstairs and be like, "Is it really noticeable today?" And even when she says no, I have to ask again, just to be sure, making her look from different sides. It's like I have to do all of these steps in order just to try and feel okay enough to walk out the door. But the crazy part is, it rarely even helps. And like I mentioned, I'll do this for so long that I end up just missing my lab completely. Or, you know, if I do manage to break the loop and finally leave, I show up so completely wiped out from all the stressing and checking that I can't even focus on my G-code or my machine setups. My brain is just fried before the day even starts.
Do you think your concerns about your face are interfering with your ability to enjoy or participate in activities that you used to find pleasurable?

Yeah, I mean, that's exactly what I was trying to explain earlier when I was talking about the soccer and the community center. It’s completely ruined all of that for me. 

I used to absolutely love playing soccer. It wasn't even super competitive, just those intramural pickup games, but it was the highlight of my week. It was my way to blow off steam after staring at screens and writing code all day, just hanging out with the guys from my classes. But I had to stop. I completely stopped going because I just can't handle the thought of people looking at me. When you're out on the field, you're totally exposed, you know? You're sweating, the sun is hitting your face from all these harsh angles, and I couldn't even focus on the ball because my brain was just screaming at me about how terrible and lopsided my jaw must look to everyone on the sidelines. It just stripped all the fun out of it. Same with the volunteering. I genuinely liked helping people with their tech issues at the community center, it felt good to use my skills, but sitting across a desk from someone while they just stare at my face... I couldn't take it anymore. I just don't want people looking at me. 

And it’s bleeding into the stuff I used to love about my actual major, too. Like, I’m a CNC guy. I love being in the shop. I love the precision of it, setting up the machines, getting the tooling right, watching a piece of raw metal turn into a perfect part. That used to be the best part of my day. But like I told you, I’ve been missing so many of my CNC labs and my shop shifts because I literally couldn’t get myself out the door. The anxiety just paralyzes me. 

And the worst part is, it's actually destroying my future. I mentioned my faculty mentor pulling me aside—he was really serious about it. He sat me down and told me point-blank that my work placement is in serious jeopardy if I don't start showing up. And that placement is everything. If I lose that, I lose the connections, the hands-on experience, basically my whole shot at a good programming job right out of school. I know all of this. I know exactly what's at stake. But the fear of people looking at my jaw is just so overwhelming that it drowns out everything else. I just sit on the edge of my bed, watching the clock tick past the start of my lab, feeling completely sick to my stomach because I know I'm throwing my life away, but I still can't force myself to go in. It just takes the joy and the drive out of absolutely everything.
Do you feel like you have to repeat any of these checking or fixing behaviors a specific number of times to feel okay about your face?

Well, I don't know if it's a specific, exact number... like, I don't tell myself I have to do it exactly five times or anything like that. But it is definitely a loop that just repeats and repeats until I literally run out of time. 

I know I keep bringing this up, but that whole morning routine I was just telling you about? The getting stuck in the bathroom before school? It's never just doing those things once. It's doing them over and over in this relentless cycle. Like, I'll check the bathroom mirror, right? And then I do the phone camera thing to see the unflipped version. But then, after I spend all that time trying to fix my hair or changing my shirt to hide the angle of my jaw, I can't just leave. I have to go back and check the mirror again to see if the new shirt or the new hair part actually worked. And then, obviously, I have to use the phone camera again to confirm it. 

So it's mirror, phone, hair, shirt, back to the mirror, back to the phone. My bedroom floor will literally just be covered in shirts because I just keep cycling through them, putting one on, checking, taking it off, trying another one. 

And it's the exact same thing with my mom. It's never just asking her once. I'll go downstairs, ask her if my face looks weird, she'll sigh and say no. But then I'll walk back upstairs, look in the mirror, completely doubt what she just told me, and realize I need to go back down and ask her again. I'll make her look at me in different lighting, or ask her if she's just saying it to make me feel better. 

So, no, it's not a set number of times, it's just... I keep doing it until I literally can't anymore. And that's exactly why I end up missing my lab entirely. The cycle just eats up the whole morning. Or, you know, if I eventually just force myself to stop and actually go to school, I'm just so incredibly wiped out. The sheer amount of times I've checked my reflection and changed my clothes and interrogated my mom... it just drains every ounce of energy out of me. By the time I get to the shop, I'm too exhausted to even focus on my work. I just can't seem to break out of that loop once it starts.
Do you feel like something bad would happen if you didn't perform these checking or fixing behaviors on your face?

Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it's not like I think the world is gonna end or I'll get into a car crash or something superstitious like that, but... the social consequence? Yeah. It would be an absolute nightmare. 

If I didn't do all that stuff I was just telling you about—you know, before I leave for school, getting stuck checking my face in the bathroom mirror, and then using my phone camera to see the real angle, and spending all that time fixing my hair or changing shirts over and over to hide the lopsidedness, and making sure to ask my mom if it looks weird... if I didn't do all of that, I literally wouldn't be able to function out in the world. It would feel like walking out into public completely naked. I'd be so incredibly exposed. 

The whole point of doing all those things is to try and put up some kind of shield, you know? To try and convince myself that maybe, just maybe, I've hidden the crookedness enough that people won't immediately stare in disgust. If I just walked out the door without checking and fixing everything, the panic would be unbearable. I'd just be standing at my CNC machine, sweating, completely convinced that every single person in the shop is staring at my jaw and judging me. I wouldn't be able to breathe. 

So I feel like I absolutely *have* to do it to protect myself, even though I know—like I keep saying—it completely backfires. Because I end up doing it for so long that I just miss my lab entirely, or, if I do manage to make it to campus, I show up so completely wiped out from the stress of the whole routine that I can't even focus on my work anyway. It's this horrible catch-22. I ruin my day by doing it, but the fear of how exposed and humiliated I'd feel if I didn't do my checks... it's just too overwhelming. I can't just not do it.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop thinking about your face, even when you try to focus on other things?

Yeah, I mean, that is literally the entire reason I finally came in to see someone. It just never stops. It doesn't matter what I'm doing or how hard I try to distract myself, my brain always circles right back to it. 

I try so hard to focus on my classes or my work, but I just can't stop thinking that the left side of my face looks completely off. Like, my nose and my jaw are just so noticeably crooked. And it's everywhere, you know? Like if I have to look at my student ID photo—which is just an absolute nightmare because the lighting is always terrible and it's completely flat so you can't hide anything—or especially in those online class cameras. Man, those are the worst. You know when you're in a remote lecture and your face is just sitting there in that little box at the bottom of the screen? I won't hear a single word the professor says for an entire hour because I'm just staring at my own square, completely obsessed with how lopsided I look, trying to tilt my head just a fraction of an inch to see if I can make it look normal. 

And the crazy thing is, even when people say they don't see it... like, I'll ask and they'll swear my face is fine, but it doesn't change anything in my head. It doesn't give me any relief at all. Because when I actually do manage to get myself into the CNC lab, trying to set up a tool path or check my tolerances, I can't even concentrate on the metal. And you have to be so dialed in when you're machining, but I just have this overwhelming, constant feeling that every single person in that lab is noticing my crooked jaw way before they ever notice my work. It's like my deformed face enters the room before I do, and it just hijacks my brain completely. So, yeah, I can't focus on anything else. It's just a constant loop playing in the background of everything I do.
Do you think your concerns about your face are significantly interfering with your daily life or relationships?

Oh, man, completely. It is... it's literally ruining everything. I mean, I know I've brought up the CNC lab a few times already, but it's not just that I'm late or that I'm a little distracted when I'm there. It's that I'm outright missing my labs and my actual shop shifts entirely because I just get so trapped in my house. I literally cannot get myself out the front door because of that whole mirror and clothes routine I was telling you about. I just get paralyzed in it. 

And the consequences are getting really real now. It's gotten so bad that my faculty mentor actually pulled me aside recently. He sat me down and told me point-blank that my work placement could be in serious jeopardy if I don't get my attendance and focus under control. Which is just... it's devastating, you know? Because I love machining, I really do, and this placement is a huge deal for my future, but I just can't force myself to go in when I feel like my face is a complete disaster. 

And it's not even just school and work, it's bleeding into literally every other part of my life, too. Like, I used to play soccer, right? Just a casual thing, but I really enjoyed it. But I had to stop. I completely quit because when you're out on the field, you're running around, you're sweating, your hair gets all messed up, and you can't hide behind anything. You can't control your angles or fix your hair when you're playing a sport. And the thought of all those guys on the team, or people on the sidelines, just staring at my face and seeing how lopsided my jaw is... I just couldn't handle it. The anxiety was too much, so I just stopped showing up. 

I even used to volunteer, too, doing some community stuff, but I dropped that for the exact same reason. I just don't want anyone looking at me. I can't stand the thought of being in a room, trying to help out or talk to people, and knowing that the person I'm talking to is just fixated on how crooked and weird my face is. It's exhausting to constantly try to hide it, so it's just easier to not go at all. So, yeah, to answer your question, it's interfering with absolutely everything. I've basically just isolated myself completely. My whole life has just shrunk down to my bedroom and my bathroom mirror because being out in the world is just too unbearable now.
Do you think your face actually looks crooked, or is it just that you feel like it does?

I mean, no, it’s not just a feeling. I genuinely believe it actually, physically looks crooked. It’s not just some... some insecurity I’ve made up in my head. 

Like I was saying before, the whole reason I finally came in to see you is because I can't stop thinking about how the left side of my face is just structurally off. It's a physical reality. My nose and my jaw are visibly crooked. I know I mentioned that other people will sometimes swear they don’t see it, but honestly? I just think people say that to be polite, you know? Or they just don't want to make things awkward by admitting how bad it is. Because when I look at those ID photos or the online class cameras I was telling you about... the camera doesn’t lie. The lens captures exactly what is physically there, and what is there is completely lopsided. You can't just "feel" like your bone structure is wrong when you can literally trace the asymmetry on a screen. 

So when I’m trying to get myself into the CNC lab, I’m not just dealing with a bad feeling. I am walking in fully aware that my face is deformed. That’s why I have that constant obsession that everyone in the shop is noticing my jaw way before they ever notice my work. Because they are. They have to be. It’s right there on my face. If it was just a feeling, I think I could maybe talk myself out of it, or, I don't know, take a deep breath and push through it. But because it’s real, because my nose and jaw actually pull to the side like that... it just makes it impossible to ignore. It's just so frustrating when people try to tell me it's just in my head, because I can literally see it with my own two eyes.
Do you think that others can see the crookedness in your face as clearly as you do?

I mean, yeah. I absolutely do. I know I just mentioned that people will sometimes say they don't see it when I ask them, but... I mean, come on. They have to see it. Like I said, the whole reason I finally came in to get help is because I literally cannot stop thinking about how the left side of my face looks completely off. It’s not a subtle thing to me at all. My nose and my jaw are just so visibly crooked, especially when you look at those ID photos or on the online class cameras where everything is just flattened out and you can't hide anything. 

And my thing is, if a terrible laptop camera can pick up exactly how lopsided I am, how could a real person standing two feet in front of me not see it? They see it. They just don't want to be rude, you know? It's basic human nature. Nobody wants to look at a guy and say, "Yeah, wow, your jaw is actually really messed up." So they lie to be polite. Or they try to downplay it to make me feel better. But I can tell. 

When I'm in the CNC lab, even if someone swears they didn't notice anything, I can feel their eyes on me. I just have this intense, unshakable feeling that every single person in that shop is noticing my face way before they ever notice my work. I'll be standing there at the machine, just trying to run a program or check my measurements, and a classmate will walk over to grab a tool or ask a question, and I just know they're staring at my jaw. I can literally feel them looking at the asymmetry. They might try to act natural, but it's just too glaring to miss. So yeah, even when people say they don't see it, I know they do. It's just so obvious to me, so it has to be obvious to them. They're definitely seeing exactly what I'm seeing.
Do you think that a plastic surgeon or a professional who specializes in facial structure would agree with your assessment of your face being crooked?

I actually think about that a lot, to be honest. Going to a plastic surgeon, I mean. Because they're trained to see millimeters of difference, right? They understand symmetry and anatomy and all that. So if I sat down in a surgeon's chair, they wouldn't do that whole polite routine that everyone else does. They wouldn't just brush it off or try to make me feel better. 

Because, like I keep coming back to—and I know I've said this a bunch, but it's the entire reason I came in to see you in the first place—I just cannot stop thinking about how the left side of my face is just completely off. My nose, my jaw, they're undeniably crooked. And a surgeon would look at the exact same ID photos I look at, or those awful online class cameras that just flatten everything out and expose every single flaw, and they would point right to the exact problem areas. They'd probably take out a ruler or some calipers and measure it, and they'd be able to show me exactly how far my jaw is swinging to the left. They would prove it. 

Because even when regular people say they don't see it, a professional would validate that it is physically there. They'd understand exactly why I feel like everyone in the CNC lab is noticing my face way before they ever notice my work. A surgeon would get it because they'd see the exact same structural defect I'm seeing, without all the social filter stuff. They wouldn't lie to me. They would see exactly what I see every single time I look at a screen, and they would know exactly why it's driving me crazy. I really think a consultation with someone like that would just confirm everything I've been telling you.
Have you considered seeking a professional opinion from a plastic surgeon or a dermatologist to assess the symmetry of your face?

I mean, yeah, I've considered it. I've thought about it a lot, actually. I haven't done it yet, though. I haven't actually made an appointment or gone in to see anyone. It's like... I think about it constantly, right? I'll be sitting there in front of my computer, looking at the camera feed, just analyzing my jaw and my nose, and I'll think, "I should just go. I should just find a specialist, someone who does facial reconstruction or whatever, and have them look at it." Because, like I said, they would know. They would have the tools to measure it and they could finally just say, "Yes, you are right, it is crooked." 

But then I start thinking about the actual process of doing it. Like, making the call, sitting in the waiting room, having to explain to the receptionist why I'm there... and then actually sitting in the chair while the doctor examines me. And honestly, the thought of someone scrutinizing my face that closely, even a professional, is just really overwhelming. It's like, I want the validation, I want someone to acknowledge that it's real and not just in my head, but at the same time, having someone point out exactly how messed up it is, in clinical terms... I don't know if I'm ready for that. 

Plus, there's the whole financial side of it. I'm just a student, I'm working part-time, trying to get through my CNC certification. I don't have the money for cosmetic consultations or surgery right now. And even if I did, what if they tell me it's too complicated to fix? Or what if they suggest some crazy invasive surgery that I can't afford or that would take me out of classes for months? So, I just end up circling back to the same spot. I think about it, I want to do it, but I just haven't actually taken that step yet. I just keep staring at those ID photos and wishing it wasn't an issue in the first place, you know?
Do you think a photographer or someone skilled in taking portraits would be able to take a picture of you where your face looks symmetrical?

I mean... I don't really see how they could. Like, I get what you're asking, because I know photographers understand lighting and angles and forced perspective and all those tricks, right? And I've actually gone down rabbit holes online reading about that stuff—like how different focal lengths, like an 85-millimeter lens versus the terrible wide-angle lens on a laptop, can change how a face looks. So I've thought, okay, maybe a professional with a ten-thousand-dollar camera setup could do something. 

But... no. Honestly, no, I don't think they could actually make it look symmetrical. Because at the end of the day, it's not just a bad angle or a trick of the light. It's the actual, physical bone structure. It's the reality of what's sitting there in front of the lens. If a photographer tries to shoot me from the right side, maybe using heavy shadows to completely hide the left side of my face... well, they aren't making it symmetrical, are they? They're just actively hiding how crooked my jaw is. They're just covering it up. And if they have to take a straight-on portrait, like for a professional headshot or something? There is literally no amount of soft lighting or bouncing the flash that is going to physically move my nose back to the center of my face. 

I just analyze this stuff constantly. In my CNC classes, when I'm looking at CAD models or checking tolerances, everything has to be perfectly aligned. You can't fake symmetry in a machine part, and you can't fake it on a face either. I mean, sure, a photographer could use Photoshop, right? They could take the file into editing software and use the warp tool to literally drag my jawline over a few millimeters in post-production. But straight out of the camera? Just a raw photo? No way. The lens just captures light bouncing off whatever is there, and what's there is completely lopsided. 

So even if the best portrait photographer in the world set up the perfect studio, the second that shutter clicks, the raw image is still going to show my left side being completely off. You just... you can't photograph your way out of an actual structural defect, you know? It's there, no matter who's holding the camera.
Do you think a professional photographer could take a picture of you where your face appears symmetrical without using any photo editing software?

Like I was just saying, if they can't use Photoshop or any editing software? Then absolutely not. Zero chance. Because... well, I know I keep circling back to this, but it’s literally the entire reason I came in to see you today. I just can’t stop thinking about it. I can't stop thinking about how the left side of my face just looks completely off. It’s right there in the physical structure. My nose and my jaw are just... they're crooked. 

And it doesn’t matter who is taking the picture or how good their equipment is. It’s in every single ID photo I’ve ever had to take, it’s glaringly obvious on those awful online class cameras when I have to log in for lectures, it's just always there. The lens just captures what physically exists. And what exists is crooked. 

And it drives me absolutely insane because it completely takes over my life. Even when my family or other people try to be nice and say they don’t see it, I know they’re just lying to make me feel better. Because I feel the judgment constantly. Like, when I walk into the CNC lab for my coursework? I can’t even focus on programming the machines because I just feel like everyone in the lab is staring at me. I feel like they are all noticing how messed up my face is way before they ever notice my work or look at the parts I'm milling. It’s like I walk in and my lopsided jaw is the very first thing that enters the room. 

In machining, if a part is out of tolerance by even a millimeter, you scrap it. It's defective. And that's exactly how I feel about my face. So no, a photographer couldn't hide that without software. It's just too defective. I just... I can't turn off the thought that everyone is looking at it, and a raw photo is only going to prove me right.
Do you think that a medical professional, such as a plastic surgeon, would agree that your face is significantly crooked?

Yeah, I mean, they would have to. A plastic surgeon is trained to measure things exactly, right? They look at the actual bone structure, the geometry of it all. So if they looked at me, they would see exactly what I’ve been talking about. They'd probably take one look and know exactly how many millimeters my jaw is shifted to the left. 

And... I know I keep bringing this all back to the same thing, but like I said, this is literally the whole reason I came in to see you today. I just... I can’t stop thinking about it. The thoughts just never turn off. I can't stop thinking about how the left side of my face just looks completely off. 

I know I mentioned the ID photos and the online class cameras earlier, but it’s because it’s just so undeniable when I look at them. My nose and my jaw are just visibly crooked. And the thing is, even when people in my life try to tell me they don’t see it, I know they're just lying. They're just being polite because they don't want to make me feel bad. But a medical professional wouldn't have to be polite, they'd just look at the asymmetry and agree with me. 

Because I know other people see it. I feel it every single day. Like I was saying about being in the CNC lab... it's not just that I feel uncomfortable, it's that it completely overshadows everything else about me. I'll be standing there, trying to run a complex program on the mill, and I just feel like everyone in the lab is noticing my face before they ever notice my work. Like, they aren't looking at the precise cuts I'm making or the tolerances I'm holding, they're just staring at my lopsided jaw. It’s like my messed-up face enters the room and introduces itself before my actual skills do. 

It's exhausting to live like that, just constantly knowing everyone is looking at this huge defect. So, yeah, if random guys in my machining class are noticing it instead of looking at my projects, a highly trained plastic surgeon is definitely going to agree that it’s significantly crooked. They'd probably wonder why I haven't gotten it fixed yet.
Do you think your perception of your face being crooked might be different from how others actually see you?

I mean... I guess I understand why you’re asking that, because, yeah, people do try to tell me that. Like I mentioned before, people will swear up and down that they don’t see it.
